title: Episode 55: The Ringling Brothers and the Baraboo Circus Dynasty
description:
The Ringling Brothers and the Baraboo Circus Dynasty: How five sons of an immigrant German harness maker built the greatest circus empire in human history from a muddy riverbank in Baraboo, Wisconsin. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of American showmanship, family integrity, and rail logistics.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the small river town of Baraboo, Wisconsin, in the eighteen seventies, five young brothers watched a paddlewheel steamboat dock along the upper Mississippi River carrying a traveling menagerie of exotic caged animals. That single childhood glimpse ignited an empire. Beginning with an old dancing bear, homemade costumes, and an old wooden farm wagon, the Ringling brothers revolutionized American entertainment, outmaneuvering P.T. Barnum and transforming the circus into a ninety-car railroad colossus that entertained millions across the globe. George brings us the colorful story of Wisconsin's circus kings.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: FIVE BOYS ON THE RIVERBANK
In the eighteen seventies, the quiet sandstone bluffs and oak groves of Baraboo, Wisconsin, were home to the family of August Rungeling, an industrious German immigrant harness maker who had crossed the Atlantic seeking honest frontier labor. August and his wife Marie raised seven sons and a daughter in a humble clapboard home where physical toil was constant and spare pennies were exceptionally rare. The boys helped in their father shop after school, cutting heavy leather reins, riveting brass buckles, and learning the values of precision and pride in manual work. But five of their sons—Al, Otto, Alf, Charles, and John—were dreamers possessed by an insatiable hunger for the theatrical stage. When a visiting riverboat circus docked in nearby McGregor, Iowa, the boys were permitted to watch the unloading of painted wooden wagons containing roaring lions, acrobats in glittering sequins, and giant African elephants marching in trunk-to-tail lines along the muddy riverbanks. The wonder of that afternoon stayed with the brothers forever, sparking an imaginative fire that would reshape American culture. Returning home to Baraboo, they began practicing juggling with turnip roots and stones, walking rope lines stretched taut between backyard apple trees, and staging amateur variety skits for neighborhood children in their father harness shop for a single copper penny or a handful of brass pins. The boys spent long summer afternoons practicing on the river bluffs, learning to tumble in the soft clover and sewing ragged canvas scraps into miniature circus pavilions. August Rungeling instilled in his boys a strict reverence for honest craftsmanship and unbreakable family loyalty, insisting that a man commercial word was his most sacred bond, a moral foundation that would later govern the greatest entertainment empire in American history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE HALL SHOW AND THE FIRST WAGON
By eighteen eighty-two, the brothers were determined to turn their childhood passion into a professional commercial business. They pooled their meager savings and organized the Ringling Brothers Classic and Comic Concert Company. Touring small rural schoolhouses, country churches, and drafty town halls across central Wisconsin, Al juggled heavy cast-iron plates and balanced plowshares on his chin, John sang humorous comic ballads and danced in oversized clown shoes, Otto played the bass viol, and Alf recited dramatic theatrical monologues. They traveled in a single spring wagon pulled by two weary farm horses, sleeping in livery stables, haylofts, and beneath the wagon box when ticket sales fell short in lean prairie villages. Midwestern townspeople and farmers were charmed by the clean humor and impressive athletic feats, spreading word across the county that the Ringling show was an honest, uplifting spectacle. The brothers possessed two secret weapons that set them apart from the shady, fly-by-night carny outfits of the era: ironclad family discipline and complete moral honesty. While rival shows tolerated crooked gambling wheels, three-card monte games, pickpockets, and short-change artists who swindled rural patrons, the Ringling brothers established a strict rule: any employee caught cheating a customer was fired on the spot. Midwestern farm families learned that a Ringling ticket promised clean, wholesome family wonder, free from coarse vulgarity or dishonest grift. Spectators arrived in horse-drawn buggies and buckboards from dozens of miles around, filling the modest benches to witness feats of athletic agility and uplifting humor that brightened their arduous frontier lives, cementing the Ringling reputation across the Upper Midwest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: TAKING TO THE CANVAS
In May eighteen eighty-four, the brothers took the ultimate financial gamble: they bought their first circus canvas tent. The modest big top seated barely six hundred patrons, and their entire menagerie consisted of an elderly blind hyena, a dancing bear, and two trained goats. The brothers divided managerial responsibilities with corporate genius that rivaled the greatest industrial barons of the gilded age. Al, the eldest, became the equestrian director, scouting acts and directing performances with an eagle eye for theatrical pacing and artistic timing. Otto was the financial wizard, known as The King, managing payroll down to the half-penny and ensuring every local merchant and hay supplier was paid in full before the show left town. Charles organized the advance advertising brigades that covered country barns, granaries, and rail fences in vivid lithograph posters weeks ahead of arrival. Alf handled press relations, writing soaring, poetic newspaper copy that romanticized the sawdust ring and captured the public imagination. And young John, blessed with razor-sharp logistical instinct, became the master of transportation, planning routes and navigating municipal ordinances across uncharted territories. Despite early hardships of flooded roads, mud-mired wagons, and shredded canvas during violent prairie squalls, their reputation for honesty caused their crowds to swell by thousands every season. Al Ringling insisted on immaculate equipment, personally inspecting every tent peg, hemp guy wire, and wooden bleacher board to guarantee the safety of the crowds who packed the benches under the kerosene lamps. Charles Ringling established an innovative advertising ledger, mapping every telegraph line, rural post office, and church parish to target promotional flyers directly to prairie families. The company strict rules of moral integrity set an unprecedented standard in the traveling entertainment industry, transforming the American circus from a disreputable sideshow into a beloved family institution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WINTER QUARTERS IN BARABOO
By the eighteen nineties, Baraboo had transformed into the official winter circus capital of the world. Along the banks of the winding Baraboo River, the Ringling brothers constructed a massive brick and timber complex covering dozens of acres: heated elephant houses, camel barns, ring barns for training acrobats, wagon construction shops, wardrobe departments, and dedicated rail maintenance sidings. Every autumn, when the traveling season ended, hundreds of exotic animals and international circus stars descended upon the quiet Wisconsin community. Townspeople grew accustomed to seeing African bull elephants being exercised down snowy residential streets and camels browsing in front yards alongside winter drifts. Local craftsmen spent the frozen Wisconsin winters carving ornate wooden wagons gilded with pure gold leaf, painting heavy wagon wheels in vibrant crimson, and sewing thousands of glittering costumes for performers and ringmasters. The Ringling winter quarters became a magical cosmopolitan enclave where Russian trapeze artists, German lion tamers, and Italian bareback riders lived side by side with Wisconsin farm folk in remarkable harmony. Ringling elephants were walked down to the Baraboo River twice daily for exercise, splashing in the cold shallows to the delight of local millworkers and school children who brought them apples and carrots. Winter preparations required months of skilled craftsmanship, as carpenters, blacksmiths, and wheelwrights labored in heated shops along the river, preparing magnificent gilded wagons for the upcoming spring tour, injecting thousands of dollars into the local economy and making Baraboo synonymous with wonder.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE IRON RAILS AND THE GOLDEN AGE
In eighteen ninety, the Ringlings made the bold decision to abandon horse-drawn mud wagons forever and take to the iron rails. John Ringling designed a revolutionary rail transport system that allowed the colossal show to dismantle in one city at midnight, load onto sixty custom flatcars and Pullman sleepers, travel one hundred miles in the pitch dark, and erect a sprawling city of canvas in a brand-new town before dawn. Their main big top could seat fifteen thousand spectators under three football fields of waterproof canvas, illuminated by private electrical dynamo plants when most American homes still relied on kerosene. The Ringlings introduced three rings of simultaneous spectacle, an immense four-pole menagerie containing polar bears, giraffes, hippopotamuses, and an eighty-piece military band led by master cornetists. When rival circus king James A. Bailey of Barnum and Bailey took his show on an extended tour of Europe in eighteen ninety-eight, the Ringling brothers boldly swept into the lucrative eastern metropolitan markets, conquering New York, Boston, and Philadelphia, and proving that the farm boys from Baraboo were now the undisputed monarchs of world entertainment. Special advance advertising railcars traveled weeks ahead of the main train, covering wooden grain elevators, brick warehouses, and rural barns in thousands of square feet of dazzling full-color lithograph posters. The colossal enterprise operated with military logistics, coordinating railroad schedules and commissary trains to feed thousands of workers and hundreds of performing animals across the continent with clockwork precision.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BARNUM & BAILEY COUP
In nineteen oh-six, following the sudden death of James A. Bailey, the Ringling brothers pulled off the ultimate entertainment coup: they purchased the legendary Barnum and Bailey circus for four hundred and ten thousand dollars in cash, paid directly on the barrelhead. For over a decade, the brothers operated both colossal shows as separate traveling entities, dominating the entire North American continent and employing thousands of artists, canvasmen, and train crews. In nineteen nineteen, facing severe wartime railroad restrictions, fuel shortages, and rising operating expenses during World War I, John Ringling merged the two behemoths into the immortal Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Combined Shows: The Greatest Show on Earth. Traveling on ninety double-length steel railroad cars with an army of over twelve hundred performers and crew, the merged circus was an American cultural institution without parallel, greeted in every city by roaring civic parades, brass bands, and officially closed school districts so children could witness the arrival of the big top. The acquisition of Barnum and Bailey united the two greatest entertainment brands in history, creating an American entertainment colossus that operated with military precision across two continents, proving that the sons of an immigrant harness maker had outsmarted every mogul on Wall Street and built a lasting commercial empire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RINGLING LEGACY AND CIRCUS WORLD
Eventually, the harsh Wisconsin winters and the need for deeper seaport access led the show to relocate its winter quarters to Sarasota, Florida, in nineteen twenty-seven. Yet the soul of the circus never left the bluffs of the Baraboo River. Today, the original brick winter quarters in Baraboo are preserved as Circus World Museum, a National Historic Landmark that houses the world largest collection of authentic antique circus wagons, hand-carved calliopes, and colorful advertising lithographs. Every summer, visitors gather on the green banks of the river to hear the steam calliope play its piercing melodies, watch magnificent horse teams pull heavy wagons through the historic streets, and celebrate the five immigrant harness maker sons who proved that with boundless imagination, relentless integrity, and fraternal unity, small-town American dreamers could conquer the entertainment capitals of the world. Today, the calliope music echoing across the Baraboo River honors five immigrant sons who transformed a childhood dream on a riverbank into an enduring global legacy of joy, spectacle, and wonder that captivated generations of American families.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Ringling Brothers built an empire of wonder that defined American entertainment for over a century. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we investigate the firestorm that incinerated Chicago and the myth of Mrs. O'Leary's cow.
